In [[theoretical computer science]], '''multiparty communication complexity''' is the study of [[communication complexity]] in the setting where there are more than two players.

In the traditional two-party [[communication complexity|communication game]], introduced by {{harvtxt|Yao|1979}},<ref>{{citation
 | last = Yao | first = Andrew Chi-Chih | author-link = Andrew Yao
 | contribution = Some complexity questions related to distributive computing
 | doi = 10.1145/800135.804414
 | pages = 209–213
 | title = Proceedings of the 11th [[ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing]] (STOC '79)
 | year = 1979| s2cid = 999287 | doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> two players, ''P''<sub>1</sub> and ''P''<sub>2</sub> attempt to compute a Boolean function 

: <math>f(x_1,x_2):\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\  x_1,x_2\in\{0,1\}^{n'},\  2n'=n</math>

Player ''P''<sub>1</sub> knows the value of ''x''<sub>2</sub>, ''P''<sub>2</sub> knows the value of ''x''<sub>1</sub>, but ''P''<sub>''i''</sub> does not know the value of ''x''<sub>''i''</sub>, for ''i''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1,&nbsp;2. 

In other words, the players know the other's variables, but not their own. The minimum number of bits that must be communicated by the players to compute ''f'' is the [[communication complexity]] of ''f'', denoted by&nbsp;''κ''(''f'').

The multiparty communication game, defined in 1983,<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Chandra | first1 = Ashok K. | author1-link = Ashok K. Chandra
 | last2 = Furst | first2 = Merrick L.
 | last3 = Lipton | first3 = Richard J. | author3-link = Richard J. Lipton
 | contribution = Multi-party protocols
 | doi = 10.1145/800061.808737
 | pages = 94–99
 | title = Proceedings of the 15th ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC '83)
 | year = 1983| isbn = 978-0-89791-099-6 | s2cid = 18180950 }}.</ref> is a powerful generalization of the two-party case: Here the players know all the others' input, except their own. Because of this property, sometimes this model is called "numbers on the forehead" model, since if the players were seated around a round table, each wearing their own input on the forehead, then every player would see all the others' input, except their own.

The formal definition is as follows: <math>k</math> players: <math>P_1, P_2,..., P_k</math> intend to compute a Boolean function 

: <math>f(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n):\{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}</math>

On set <math>S=\{x_1, x_2,..., x_n\} </math> of variables there is a fixed partition <math>A</math> of <math>k</math> classes <math>A_1,A_2,...,A_k</math>, and player <math>P_i</math> knows every variable, ''except'' those in <math>A_i</math>, for <math>i=1,2,...,k</math>. The players have unlimited computational power, and they  communicate with the help of a blackboard, viewed by all players.

The aim is to compute <math>f(x_1,x_2,...,x_n</math>), such  that at the end of the computation, every player knows this value. The cost of the computation is the number of bits written onto the blackboard for the given input  <math>x=(x_1,x_2,...,x_n)</math> and partition <math>A=(A_1,A_2,...,A_n)</math>. The cost of a multiparty protocol is the maximum number of bits communicated for any <math>x</math> from the set {0,1}<sup>''n''</sup> and the given partition <math>A</math>. The <math>k</math>-party communication complexity, <math>C^{(k)}_A (f)</math> of a function <math>f</math>, with respect to partition <math>A</math>, is the minimum of costs of those <math>k</math>-party protocols which compute <math>f</math>. The <math>k</math>-party symmetric communication complexity of <math>f</math> is defined as 

: <math>C^{(k)}(f)=\max_AC^{(k)}_A(f) </math>

where the maximum is taken over all ''k''-partitions of set <math>x=(x_1,x_2,...,x_n)</math>.

== Upper and lower bounds ==

For a general upper bound both for two and more players, let us suppose that ''A''<sub>1</sub> is one of the smallest classes  of the partition ''A''<sub>1</sub>,''A''<sub>2</sub>,...,''A''<sub>''k''</sub>. Then ''P''<sub>1</sub> can compute any [[Boolean function]] of ''S'' with |''A''<sub>1</sub>|&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 bits of communication: ''P''<sub>2</sub> writes down the |''A''<sub>1</sub>| bits of ''A''<sub>1</sub> on the blackboard, ''P''<sub>1</sub> reads it, and computes and announces the value <math>f(x)</math>. So, the following can be written:

: <math>C^{(k)}(f)\leq\bigg\lfloor{n\over k}\bigg\rfloor+1.</math>

The Generalized Inner Product function (GIP)<ref name="BNS">{{citation
 | last1 = Babai | first1 = László | author1-link = László Babai
 | last2 = Nisan | first2 = Noam | author2-link = Noam Nisan
 | last3 = Szegedy | first3 = Márió | author3-link = Mario Szegedy
 | doi = 10.1016/0022-0000(92)90047-M
 | issue = 2
 | journal = [[Journal of Computer and System Sciences]]
 | mr = 1186884
 | pages = 204–232
 | title = Multiparty protocols, pseudorandom generators for logspace, and time-space trade-offs
 | volume = 45
 | year = 1992| doi-access = 
 }}.</ref> is defined as follows:
Let <math>y_1,y_2,...,y_k</math> be <math>n</math>-bit vectors, and let <math>Y</math> be the <math>n</math> times <math>k</math> matrix, with <math>k</math> columns as the <math>y_1,y_2,...,y_k</math> vectors. Then <math>GIP(y_1,y_2,...,y_k)</math> is the number of the all-1 rows of matrix <math>Y</math>, taken modulo&nbsp;2. In other words, if the vectors <math>y_1,y_2,...,y_k</math> correspond to the [[Eigenvalues and eigenvectors|characteristic vectors]] of <math>k</math> subsets of an <math>n</math> element base-set, then GIP corresponds to the [[Parity (mathematics)|parity]] of the intersection of these <math>k</math> subsets.

It was shown<ref name="BNS" /> that

: <math>C^{(k)}(GIP)\geq c {n\over4^k},</math>

with a constant&nbsp;''c''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0.

An upper bound on the multiparty communication complexity of GIP shows<ref>{{citation
 | last = Grolmusz | first = Vince
 | doi = 10.1006/inco.1994.1051
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[Information and Computation]]
 | mr = 1277711
 | pages = 51–54
 | title = The BNS lower bound for multi-party protocols is nearly optimal
 | volume = 112
 | year = 1994| doi-access = free
 }}.</ref> that

: <math>C^{(k)}(GIP)\leq c {n\over2^k},</math>

with a constant ''c''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0.

For a general Boolean function ''f'', one can bound the multiparty communication complexity of ''f'' by using its ''L''<sub>1</sub> norm<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Bruck | first1 = Jehoshua
 | last2 = Smolensky | first2 = Roman
 | doi = 10.1137/0221003
 | issue = 1
 | journal = [[SIAM Journal on Computing]]
 | mr = 1148813
 | pages = 33–42
 | title = Polynomial threshold functions, AC<sup>0</sup> functions, and spectral norms
 | volume = 21
 | year = 1992| url = http://authors.library.caltech.edu/30356/1/BRUfocs90.pdf
 }}.</ref> as follows:<ref>{{citation
 | last = Grolmusz | first = V.
 | doi = 10.1007/PL00009265
 | issue = 4
 | journal = [[Algorithmica]]
 | mr = 1673395
 | pages = 341–353
 | title = Harmonic analysis, real approximation, and the communication complexity of Boolean functions
 | volume = 23
 | year = 1999| s2cid = 26779824
 }}.</ref>

: <math>C^{(k)}(f) = O\Bigg(k^2\log(n L_1(f))\Bigg\lceil{n L_1^2(f)\over2^k}\Bigg\rceil\Bigg)</math>

== Multiparty communication complexity and pseudorandom generators==

A construction of a [[pseudorandom number generator]] was based on the BNS lower bound for the GIP function.<ref name="BNS" />
